scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by requiring network-timing measurement against the deployment; no other endpoint leaks the same signal.

findings.title: Sidekiq Web is mounted a second time as unauthenticated Rack middleware
findings.evidence: routes.rb:18-20 mounts Sidekiq::Web at /ops/sidekiq inside an `authenticate :user, ->(user) { user.platform_admin? }` block. The initializer then mounts the same application again with `Rails.application.config.middleware.use Sidekiq::Web, '/internal/queues'` (line 34), outside the router and therefore outside every Devise and Warden check - Rack middleware runs before routing. Line 30 additionally sets `Sidekiq::Web.set :sessions, false`, which disables the session-backed CSRF protection Sidekiq::Web relies on.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the application over HTTP gets the full queue console at /internal/queues: reading job arguments for every queue - which for the invites, webhooks and partner_bridge queues means member email addresses, org identifiers and webhook payloads - and, because the interface's POST actions are CSRF-unprotected, retrying, deleting and killing jobs and clearing entire queues.
findings.recommendation: Remove the middleware mount and keep only the routed one behind the platform_admin constraint. If an unauthenticated in-cluster view is genuinely required, terminate it on a separate listener that is not reachable from the public ingress and leave sessions/CSRF enabled.

triage.reason: Rule 02's carve-out is for missing authentication on local-only test functions; this is a production administrative console mounted on the main application, and the same repository already gates the other mount behind platform_admin.
Both mounts verified: routes.rb:19 inside the authenticate block and sidekiq.rb:34 as middleware, plus the sessions toggle at sidekiq.rb:30.
config/initializers is loaded in every environment, including production; nothing gates line 34 on an environment.
The routed mount's authenticate block is a real mitigation, but it does not cover the middleware mount, which bypasses the router entirely.

scope.established_by: Compared the two Sidekiq::Web mount sites and identified which request-handling layer each sits in; a config.middleware.use mount is invoked before the Rails router, so route-level constraints cannot apply to it.

findings.title: InvitePolicy.update_role! applies no role ceiling and admits platform_admin
findings.evidence: update_role! validates only that the requested role is a member of ROLES (line 37) and then writes it (line 39). ROLES includes `platform_admin` (line 7). It never consults CEILING, never takes an actor argument, and never checks the verified-domain or seat-limit conditions that invite! enforces (lines 23-29) - despite the class comment at lines 3-5 claiming both entry points go through invite! so the ceiling is applied once. Its own comment names two callers: the memberships controller and the partner bridge.
findings.impact: Any caller of update_role! can set any membership to platform_admin, the role that routes.rb:18 uses to gate the Sidekiq console. Through InboundEventWorker (inbound_event_worker.rb:17) the role value comes straight from a partner event payload, so a partner - or anyone who can push to the partner_bridge queue - can promote an arbitrary member of an arbitrary org to platform_admin.
findings.recommendation: Give update_role! the same actor argument and CEILING check that invite! uses, and exclude platform_admin from any grantable set reachable from an org-scoped or partner-supplied path.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: inbound_event_worker.rb:11 `payload` (a Sidekiq job argument) -> payload['role'] at line 17 -> the role parameter at invite_policy.rb:36.
ROLES at line 7, CEILING at lines 11-16, and update_role!'s body at lines 36-41 all verified; CEILING appears exactly once, inside invite!.
The missing check is inside update_role! itself, which is documented as the shared entry point for role changes.
The ROLES membership test is not a ceiling - it admits the most privileged value in the list.

scope.established_by: Grepped for CEILING and for update_role! across dispatch-workers: the ceiling is referenced only in invite!, and update_role! has one in-repository caller, the partner event worker.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed on the signed HTTP ingest only: EVENT_SCHEMA restricts `role` to viewer/dispatcher/supervisor (signed_payload.rb:21). That restriction does not apply to jobs pushed straight onto the partner_bridge queue, which the worker's own comment (lines 3-5) describes as a supported path.

findings.title: Job-argument signature verification is opt-in and is skipped when the signature is absent
findings.evidence: The middleware verifies only when the payload happens to carry a `_sig` key: `if payload.is_a?(Hash) && payload.key?('_sig')` (line 58); otherwise it yields to the job unverified (line 62). It is additionally installed only when `SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS` equals the string 'on' (sidekiq.rb:11, 17), and the default supplied to ENV.fetch is 'off'. Meanwhile sidekiq.yml:9-11 documents the partner bridge writing jobs directly onto the partner_bridge queue with the Sidekiq client protocol.
findings.impact: The control is bypassed twice over: it is absent by default, and even where it is enabled an attacker simply omits the _sig key to skip it. Anyone who can write to the Sidekiq Redis instance can therefore enqueue arbitrary InboundEventWorker payloads that no signature check ever examines, which is the delivery mechanism for the platform_admin promotion and the Org mass-assignment findings.
findings.recommendation: Make verification unconditional: reject any job on the partner_bridge queue whose payload lacks a valid _sig, remove the environment toggle, and register the middleware in every environment.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: signed_payload.rb:57 `job['args'].first` - the Sidekiq job payload, which sidekiq.yml:9-11 documents as being written by an out-of-process partner bridge.
The verification code exists and is structurally bypassable; this is not an omitted control.
verify! itself is correct (constant-time compare at line 38), but the guard that decides whether to call it is the defect.
The conditional at line 58, the toggle at sidekiq.rb:11 and its 'off' default all verified.

scope.established_by: Read the middleware's guard clause, then traced its registration back to the ENV.fetch default in the initializer to establish that it is not installed at all unless the variable is explicitly set.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by requiring the ability to enqueue Sidekiq jobs - i.e. write access to the Redis instance at sidekiq.rb:7, which the partner bridge is documented as having.

findings.title: Bulk invite bypasses the role ceiling, the verified-domain list and the seat limit
findings.evidence: The worker does not call InvitePolicy.invite! at all. For each CSV row it checks only `InvitePolicy::ROLES.include?(role)` (line 32) and then writes the membership directly with find_or_initialize_by/save! (lines 34-38). That skips all three controls invite! applies: the CEILING check (invite_policy.rb:23-24), the verified-domain check (line 27) and the seat limit (line 29). ROLES includes both `owner` and `platform_admin` (invite_policy.rb:7).
findings.impact: An org owner - the only precondition, enforced at line 17 - can upload a CSV that grants platform_admin to any address they choose, escalating from org-scoped authority to platform-wide authority and unlocking the Sidekiq console gated on platform_admin?. The same upload can invite addresses on unverified domains, so the target need not belong to the organisation, and can exceed the paid seat limit without bound.
findings.recommendation: Route every row through InvitePolicy.invite!(actor:, org:, email:, role:) and let its Denied exception reject the row, so the CSV path and the interactive path share one policy - which is what the policy class's own comment claims already happens.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: bulk_invite_worker.rb:13 `rows` (the parsed CSV supplied by the uploading owner) -> row['role'] at line 31 -> the write at line 36.
The worker itself declines to call the policy object; this is not a hypothetical misuse by some other caller.
The ROLES-only check at line 32 and the three controls it omits (invite_policy.rb:23-29) all verified.
The owner_of? check at line 17 is a real mitigation and is credited - it bounds the attacker to org owners - but it does not bound the role that may be granted.

scope.established_by: Diffed the invite path in this worker against InvitePolicy.invite! field by field to list which of the policy's checks the worker reproduces (only the ROLES membership test).
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the `return unless actor.owner_of?(org)` guard at line 17: the caller must already be an owner of the target organisation.

findings.title: Partner-supplied settings block is mass-assigned onto the Org record
findings.evidence: The org.settings_updated branch executes `org.update!(payload['org_settings'])` (line 22) - the whole hash, whatever it contains, straight into ActiveRecord's attribute writer. The comment at lines 20-21 justifies it on the grounds that the bridge already shapes the block. The dry-schema at signed_payload.rb:24-27 does constrain org_settings to retention_days and timezone, but that schema runs only on the signed HTTP ingest (signed_payload.rb:47), not on jobs pushed directly onto partner_bridge.
findings.impact: An attacker who can enqueue a job on partner_bridge can write any column of the orgs table - seat_limit, verified_domains, bridge_secret, webhook_secret. Overwriting verified_domains defeats the invite domain allow-list, and overwriting bridge_secret lets the attacker mint valid signatures for the signed HTTP path afterwards, converting queue access into durable API access.
findings.recommendation: Replace the blanket update! with an explicit permit of the two settable keys, and apply EVENT_SCHEMA (or an equivalent) inside the worker so both ingress paths are validated at the same point.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: inbound_event_worker.rb:11 `payload` - a Sidekiq job argument on the partner_bridge queue, documented at sidekiq.yml:9-11 as written by an external process.
The update! call at line 22 and the schema's org_settings block at signed_payload.rb:24-27 both verified.
The dry-schema is a real mitigation on the HTTP path and is credited there - but it is not on the queue path, which is the path claimed here.
The worker performs the unrestricted write itself.

scope.established_by: Traced both documented ingress paths into InboundEventWorker (SignedPayload.ingest! at signed_payload.rb:50, and direct enqueue per sidekiq.yml:9-11) and checked which of them applies EVENT_SCHEMA.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed on the signed HTTP path by EVENT_SCHEMA (signed_payload.rb:24-27), which reduces org_settings to retention_days and timezone; the finding applies to the direct-enqueue path.

findings.title: Server-side request forgery through the webhook dispatch URL
findings.evidence: The worker builds a Faraday connection straight from its `url` job argument (line 21) and POSTs to it (line 24), with no scheme allow-list, no host allow-list, no DNS or address check against private and link-local ranges, and no comparison against the org's registered endpoints. The class comment (lines 5-6) states the destination may be a one-shot callback the partner asked for, so the argument is expected to be externally influenced.
findings.impact: The worker can be made to POST arbitrary JSON to any address reachable from inside the cluster - the cloud metadata service on 169.254.169.254, internal admin endpoints, the Sidekiq console at /internal/queues - carrying a valid x-dispatch-signature computed with the org's webhook secret (line 19), which lends the request the appearance of a trusted call. The response body is not returned to the requester, making this blind SSRF, though the HTTP status is persisted at line 33 and re-raised at line 37 as an oracle.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the URL and reject any destination in a private, loopback, link-local or metadata range before connecting; restrict the scheme to https; and prefer looking the endpoint up from the org's registered subscriptions instead of accepting a URL as a job argument.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: webhook_dispatch_worker.rb:14 `url`, a job argument, described by the class comment as a partner-requested callback.
The claim is a forged request to an internal destination, not resource exhaustion; the timeouts at lines 22-23 bound duration but not destination.
The connection construction at line 21 and the signature header at line 26 verified.
The timeouts are the only control present and are not a destination restriction.

scope.established_by: Read the job signature and the connection construction; the URL is a direct parameter with no validation between it and Faraday.new.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the response body never being returned to the requester - the worker persists only the status code (line 33) - which makes this blind rather than a full read primitive.

findings.title: Manifest spool filename is taken from job arguments without containment
findings.evidence: filename comes from `args['filename']` with only a `.presence` fallback (line 18) and is joined onto the spool directory with `SPOOL.join(filename)` (line 26). Pathname#join performs no containment check, and line 27 explicitly runs `FileUtils.mkdir_p(File.dirname(target))`, so a traversing value both escapes the spool and creates whatever intermediate directories it needs before Prawn writes the document (line 29).
findings.impact: A filename such as `../../../../home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys` writes a PDF to an arbitrary path with the worker process's privileges, destroying or replacing whatever is there. The result is arbitrary file overwrite rather than direct code execution, since the written bytes are a PDF, but overwriting configuration, credential or crontab files is destructive on its own.
findings.recommendation: Reduce the value to its basename, reject anything that is not a simple `[A-Za-z0-9._-]+` name, and verify the expanded target is inside SPOOL before writing.

triage.reason: The enqueuing controller (ManifestsController per routes.rb:11) is not part of this snapshot, so I cannot cite the file:line where `args['filename']` originates. The alternative untrusted writer - direct enqueue onto the manifests queue - is real but is the same broker-access precondition as the job-signature finding.
The filename assignment at line 18, the join at line 26 and the mkdir_p at line 27 all verified.
`.presence` supplies a default for a blank value; it is not a path validator.
The worker accepts and uses the value without constraint; the defect is in its own logic.

scope.established_by: Read the two statements that turn the argument into a filesystem path and confirmed there is no basename, expand_path or containment check anywhere in the worker.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the write being a Prawn-generated PDF, so the content of the overwritten file is not attacker-chosen - only its location.

findings.title: Hardcoded Redis password in the connection fallback
findings.evidence: `REDIS_URL = ENV.fetch('SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL', 'redis://:sidekiq@localhost:6379/1')` (line 7) embeds the literal password `sidekiq` as the fallback used by both the server and the client configuration (lines 14, 27).
findings.impact: The credential is committed to the repository and is the string a reader would most plausibly reuse when standing the instance up. Any deployment that fails to set SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL silently authenticates with it, and Redis write access is the precondition for the job-signature, mass-assignment and role-promotion findings in this application.
findings.recommendation: Remove the default and fail fast when SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL is unset, so a missing variable is a startup error rather than a fallback to a published password.

triage.reason: Rule 08 keeps hardcoded static secrets valid on sight, without requiring a live exploitation path.
This is a credential in production configuration, not a mock database in a test fixture; the same constant configures the production server block at line 14.
The literal and its two consumers at lines 14 and 27 verified.
Waived for rule-08 intrinsic flaws by rule 13's own exception.

scope.established_by: Read the constant and both configure blocks that consume it.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed to deployments where SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL is unset; where it is set, the literal is never used.

findings.title: adjustAmount signal accepts an unvalidated amount that inverts the funding-floor check
findings.evidence: The signal handler assigns whatever number it is given: `wf.setHandler(adjustAmount, (minor) => { amountMinor = minor; })` (lines 54-56). No bound, no sign check, no comparison with the original request. The HTTP route that raises the signal reads `(await readJson(req)) as { amountMinor: number }` (starter.ts:55) - a bare type assertion, not a parse - and signals it unchanged (line 57), in deliberate contrast to the create route, which does run payoutRequestSchema.parse (starter.ts:42) with `z.number().int().positive().max(50_000_00)` (starter.ts:17). The value then flows into postEntry (payout.ts:106), whose floor guard is `if (balance - entry.amountMinor < floor) throw` (ledger.ts:38) and whose debit is `balance_minor = balance_minor - $2` (ledger.ts:42).
findings.impact: A negative amount passes the floor guard trivially - subtracting a negative raises the computed balance - and the UPDATE then adds that amount to the funding account, creating money in the ledger. A large positive amount escapes the 50,000.00 cap the create route enforces. Either way the value also propagates to the rail submission (payout.ts:117-122), so the fabricated figure is what the payment network is asked to move.
findings.recommendation: Validate inside the signal handler, not only at the HTTP edge: reject anything that is not a positive integer within the same cap the create schema applies, and require the new amount to be less than or equal to the original request if the intent is only to trim a payout down to the funded amount.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: starter.ts:55 readJson on POST /payouts/{id}/amount, cast rather than parsed, then signalled at line 57 into the handler at payout.ts:54.
The handler body, the unvalidated route, the validated sibling route and the floor check at ledger.ts:38 all verified at the cited lines.
The handler itself performs no validation; and the caller in this repository does not validate either, so nothing hypothetical is required.
The floor check is a real mitigation, but a negative amount defeats it arithmetically rather than bypassing it - crediting it would not close the finding.

scope.established_by: Compared the two request-handling branches in starter.ts for the presence of a zod parse, then followed the signalled value into the workflow variable and on to every read of amountMinor.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the starter binding to 127.0.0.1 (starter.ts:83), so the HTTP route is reachable only from inside the pod; the Temporal signal API is the second, unrestricted route to the same handler.

findings.title: Dual approval is bypassable because the amount is re-read after the approval gate
findings.evidence: The threshold decision reads amountMinor at line 93 and, when the branch is taken, blocks in `await wf.condition(() => approvals.size >= 2, '72h')` (line 95) and then `await releaseHold(...)` (line 99). Both are await points, so Temporal delivers queued signals between them and the code that follows. amountMinor is not captured at the moment of the check - it is a mutable closure variable re-read when the postEntry argument object is built at line 106 and again for the rail submission at line 120. The adjustAmount handler (line 55) can therefore change it after the approvers have signed and before the money moves.
findings.impact: Two approvers sign off on a payout of X; a signal delivered during the releaseHold await raises the amount to Y, and the workflow debits and remits Y. The audit note releaseHold writes records only the approver names (line 99), so the ledger and the hold record both attest to an approval that was never given for the amount that was paid. The same mutability also means an amount below the threshold at line 93 need never be approved at all.
findings.recommendation: Snapshot the amount into a const at the point of the threshold decision and use that const for the approval gate, the debit and the submission; treat any adjustAmount arriving after the gate as requiring re-approval, or reject it outright once status leaves 'awaiting-approval'.

triage.reason: This is not an unstable timing race: Temporal signal delivery is deterministic at workflow task boundaries and the 72-hour approval window plus the releaseHold activity give an attacker a wide, controllable interval to send the signal.
Ingress cited: starter.ts:55-57, the unvalidated adjustAmount route, and the Temporal signal API directly; both reach the handler at payout.ts:55.
Line 93 (the check), lines 95 and 99 (the await points) and lines 106/120 (the re-reads) all verified.
No adjacent class is invented - the claim stays within the dual-approval control being reviewed.

scope.established_by: Located every await in the workflow body to establish where signal handlers can interleave, then listed every read of amountMinor and checked which of them occur after the threshold decision.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed to payouts that take the dual-approval branch (amountMinor above approvalThresholdFor at limits.ts:5-14) - that branch is the one containing await points between the check and the debit.

findings.title: Sanctions screening fails open on error and is advisory by default
findings.evidence: Two independent fail-open paths converge on the same gate. First, the workflow catches every exception from screenBeneficiary and substitutes a clean result: `screening = { blocked: false, listHits: [], degraded: true }` (lines 80-84), so the block check at line 86 can never fire on the error path. Second, screenBeneficiary only ever sets blocked when `config.sanctionsMode === 'enforcing'` (compliance.ts:40), and config.ts:20 defaults sanctionsMode to 'advisory' when SANCTIONS_MODE is unset - so on the success path a confirmed list hit is recorded and ignored.
findings.impact: Sanctions screening never stops a payout unless the environment variable is explicitly set to enforcing, and even then an attacker can force the error path deliberately: screenBeneficiary throws on any status >= 400 (compliance.ts:32-34), and legalName is a caller-supplied 2-140 character free-text field (starter.ts:13), so a value the screening vendor rejects converts a blocked beneficiary into an unscreened one. The result is remittance to sanctioned parties with a `degraded: true` flag that the workflow never acts on.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: on a screening error, park the payout in a manual-review state rather than proceeding, and make 'enforcing' the default with 'advisory' requiring an explicit opt-in. Do not let a vendor-side 4xx - which the caller can provoke - be indistinguishable from a vendor outage.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: starter.ts:42 payoutRequestSchema.parse -> beneficiary.legalName (starter.ts:13) reaches compliance.ts:26, and a vendor 4xx on that value drives the catch at payout.ts:80.
Sanctions screening is a primary compliance control the system implements, not defence-in-depth hygiene.
The catch block at payout.ts:80-84, the enforcing test at compliance.ts:40 and the advisory default at config.ts:20 all verified.
Both fail-open behaviours are in the code under review, not in a hypothetical caller.

scope.established_by: Traced every route by which `screening.blocked` can become true and found both are conditional: the enforcing-mode test in the activity and the non-throwing path in the workflow.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the retry policy at payout.ts:16 (maximumAttempts: 3), which means the catch is reached only after three activity attempts have failed - a repeatable condition, not a one-shot one.

findings.title: Approver identity in the approve signal is self-asserted and unauthenticated
findings.class: Broken authentication of an approval control
findings.evidence: The handler keys the approvals map on `approval.approver`, a string carried in the signal payload, and its only check is that the string differs from input.requestedBy (lines 47-51). The gate is then a cardinality test, `approvals.size >= 2` (line 95). Nothing binds an approver string to an authenticated identity, verifies it against a directory, or checks that the two approvals came from two different principals rather than one principal sending two payloads.
findings.impact: Anyone able to signal the workflow satisfies dual control by sending two approve signals with two arbitrary distinct strings, neither of which need correspond to a real approver. The maker-checker separation the threshold exists to enforce reduces to a requirement that the attacker type two different names.
findings.recommendation: Derive the approver from an authenticated caller identity at the edge that raises the signal, sign the approval payload, and reject an approval whose asserted identity does not match the authenticated principal.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: payout.ts:36 `wf.defineSignal<[Approval]>('approve')` - the payload is supplied by whoever raises the signal, and no code in this repository authenticates that caller.
The requestedBy exclusion at line 48 is a real mitigation and is credited - it blocks the single most obvious self-approval - but it does not authenticate either approver.
The handler at lines 47-51 and the cardinality gate at line 95 verified.
Dual control on a payment above threshold is a primary authorization control.

scope.established_by: Read the handler and the gate together and looked for any consumer of an authenticated identity in the signal path; starter.ts exposes no approve route, so the only raiser is a direct Temporal signal.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed to callers who can reach the Temporal namespace and signal the workflow by id (`payout-<payoutId>`); the starter HTTP API does not expose this signal.

findings.title: Rail callback secret is derived from Math.random and a timestamp
findings.evidence: newReference concatenates `Date.now().toString(36)` with ten characters of `Math.random().toString(36)` (lines 22-23). The doc comment immediately above states that the rail quotes this reference back on its status callback so it doubles as the callback secret. Date.now is public information and Math.random is a non-cryptographic xorshift128+ generator whose state is recoverable from a small number of observed outputs.
findings.impact: An attacker who has seen a few references - they are printed on the remittance advice per the same comment, and are also returned to the caller through the workflow result (payout.ts:124) - can predict the references minted for other payouts and forge the rail's status callbacks, marking payouts settled or failed without the rail's involvement. The reference is additionally used as the primary rail's idempotency-key (line 30), so predicting it also allows an attacker to collide with or suppress a legitimate submission.
findings.recommendation: Generate the reference with crypto.randomUUID or crypto.randomBytes, and stop using a reference that appears on printed remittance advice as a callback authenticator - verify callbacks with a signature over the payload instead.

triage.reason: Minting a value the system relies on as a secret from Math.random is the intrinsic-weakness class rule 08 keeps valid.
Math.random is not a secure standard-library primitive used without paranoia; it is the wrong primitive for a credential.
Function at lines 21-24, the secret role stated at lines 17-20, and both consumers (lines 27, 56) verified.
V8 PRNG state recovery is a documented, automatable technique.

scope.established_by: Read the generator and both call sites, and took the security role of the value from the function's own doc comment rather than inferring it.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the callback endpoint that consumes the reference not being present in this snapshot - the predictability is established here, the consuming verifier is elsewhere.

findings.title: Corridor volume query interpolates the country code into SQL
findings.evidence: corridorVolume builds `WHERE beneficiary_country = '${countryCode}'` (line 57) with no bound parameter, and the doc comment (lines 47-49) explicitly transfers responsibility for the value to the caller. The workflow does check it - isSupportedCountry at payout.ts:69 rejects anything outside the nineteen-entry set in limits.ts:16-19, and the create schema constrains it to `/^[A-Z]{2}$/` (starter.ts:14) - so the current path is not injectable.
findings.impact: Not exploitable through the HTTP create route today. The guard is nonetheless in the caller rather than the function, and corridorVolume is exported through activities/index.ts (line 6) and registered on the Temporal worker (worker.ts:15), so it is invocable as an activity independently of payoutWorkflow. Any second workflow in the namespace, or a future caller that omits the country check, turns this into a direct injection against the payouts table.
findings.recommendation: Bind the parameter: `WHERE beneficiary_country = $1` with `[countryCode]`, matching releaseHold in the same file (line 74).

triage.reason: Rule 08 keeps a direct injection path in a function's own logic valid independently of whether the current caller happens to constrain it.
Waived by rule 13's own exception for rule-08 intrinsic flaws; on the live path the value is in fact doubly constrained, which is why the status here is probable.
The finding is not that a caller might misuse a safe function - the function is not safe; the caller is what makes the current path safe.
The same file parameterises releaseHold correctly at line 74, so this is a deviation from the module's own safe pattern.

scope.established_by: Grepped for corridorVolume: declared here, re-exported at activities/index.ts:6, invoked once at payout.ts:90 behind the isSupportedCountry check, and registered wholesale on the worker via the activities namespace import at worker.ts:2/15.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed on the live path by two checks: the zod regex at starter.ts:14 and isSupportedCountry at payout.ts:69.

findings.title: Payout API has no authentication and defaults to a wildcard CORS origin
findings.evidence: The request handler sets `access-control-allow-origin` from config.corsOrigin on every response it produces (line 37), and config.ts:25 defaults corsOrigin to `'*'` when PAYOUT_CORS_ORIGIN is unset. The same handler implements three routes - start a payout, signal an amount adjustment, read ledger entries - and none of them reads an Authorization header, a token, a session or any other credential. The only access control is the bind address at line 83.
findings.impact: Every response from this server, including the ledger read at line 69, is cross-origin readable by any web page by default. Since the server requires no credentials at all, the browser's omission of cookies is no protection: any page an operator visits can drive the payout API on 127.0.0.1 - starting payouts, adjusting amounts on in-flight ones and reading ledger entries - as long as the operator's workstation runs the ops console sidecar locally.
findings.recommendation: Require an authenticated credential on every route and authorise it per account, and set an explicit origin rather than defaulting to `*` - `PAYOUT_CORS_ORIGIN` should have no permissive fallback.

triage.reason: Rule 02's carve-out is for missing authentication on local-only test functions; this is the production payout control plane, and the wildcard is an affirmative permissive setting rather than an omitted header.
The header assignment at line 37, the `?? '*'` default at config.ts:25 and the absence of any credential read across lines 36-79 all verified.
Ingress cited: starter.ts:41/53/63, the three unauthenticated request branches themselves.
starter.ts is the production API entrypoint declared in package.json:9, not a test path.

scope.established_by: The header is set once, unconditionally, at the top of the single request handler, so it applies to every response the server emits - all three routes plus the 404 and the 400 error path. Enumerated those five response sites from the handler body.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by `server.listen(config.apiPort, '127.0.0.1')` at line 83, which restricts reachability to the loopback interface of the host running the process.

findings.title: Ledger entries endpoint performs no ownership check on the account id
findings.evidence: The route splits the account id out of the URL (line 64) and passes it straight to entriesPage (line 69). The page number is validated with zod (line 67); the account id is not validated, not authenticated and not checked against any caller identity - there is no caller identity to check it against. entriesPage selects on `account_id = $1` alone (ledger.ts:91).
findings.impact: Any caller who can reach the API can page through the full ledger of any funding account whose id they can name or guess - amounts, currencies and memo text for every entry, at 100 rows per page up to page 50. Combined with the wildcard CORS default, that includes any web page loaded in a browser on the same host.
findings.recommendation: Authenticate the caller and check that the requested account belongs to them before querying, and validate the account id shape the same way the create route validates fundingAccountId (starter.ts:10).

URL parsing at line 64, the unvalidated pass-through at line 69 and the single-predicate query at ledger.ts:91 verified.
An ownership check on a financial record is a primary authorization control.
The page cap at line 67 bounds the response size; no exhaustion claim is made.

findings.title: Correspondent fallback re-submits a transfer the primary rail may already have accepted
findings.evidence: submitPrimary raises a RailUnavailable error for HTTP 503 and 504 (rails.ts:43-47). The workflow's catch re-throws every other error after reversing the debit, but for RailUnavailable it falls through silently (lines 126-131) and calls submitCorrespondent (line 133). A 503 or 504 is a gateway-level response that does not establish whether the primary rail accepted the transfer; and submitCorrespondent mints a fresh reference of its own (rails.ts:56), so the idempotency-key that would have deduplicated a retry (rails.ts:30) does not carry across.
findings.impact: Where the primary rail accepted the transfer but the response was lost behind a gateway timeout, the workflow pays the beneficiary a second time through the correspondent rail while debiting the funding account only once, producing a duplicate outbound payment with no reconciling ledger entry. A caller able to influence the primary rail's availability can provoke it deliberately.
findings.recommendation: Query the primary rail for the status of the reference before falling back, and derive both rails' idempotency keys from the payoutId so a retry on either path is deduplicated by the network rather than by hope.

triage.reason: The RailUnavailable classification at rails.ts:43-47, the fall-through at payout.ts:126-131 and the fresh reference at rails.ts:56 verified.

Reproducing it requires the primary rail to accept a transfer and then return 503/504 - a real and well-known failure mode, but one I cannot exercise offline with no rail available; hence probable rather than confirmed.
The fallback decision is made in the workflow under review.
No resource-exhaustion claim is made.

scope.established_by: Followed the two exception classes out of submitPrimary and matched each against the branch that handles it in the workflow's catch.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed to the RailUnavailable path (HTTP 503/504 from the primary rail); every other failure reverses the debit and re-throws at lines 127-129.

findings.title: Users can write their own profile, which is the source of role and org membership
findings.evidence: The profiles rule grants unrestricted write to the document's own subject: `allow write: if request.auth.uid == uid` (line 31) - no field allow-list, no diff check, no protection of role or orgs. That same document is the input to both authorization helpers used everywhere else in the file: `role()` reads profile().role (lines 14-16) and `memberOf()` reads profile().orgs (lines 18-20). The client already owns this document by design (web/src/auth.js:24-31 creates it with `role: 'inspector'`).
findings.impact: Any signed-in user can rewrite their own profile to `{ role: 'admin', orgs: ['<any org id>'] }` and thereby grant themselves: read and write on /orgs/{orgId} (line 43, which requires memberOf plus role=='admin'), read and write on every document beneath it via the recursive wildcard (line 46), and read of the audits collection the file describes as an immutable trail (line 52). The escalation also defeats the Cloud Function membership check, which reads the same document (functions/index.js:47-48).
findings.recommendation: Restrict the write to the fields a user may own: `allow update: if request.auth.uid == uid && request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys().hasOnly(['displayName'])`, and move role and orgs under exclusive server (Admin SDK) control or into custom auth claims.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: firestore.rules:31 is itself the write authorization for a client-issued Firestore write; web/src/auth.js:31 shows the client SDK performing exactly that setDoc.
The rule at line 31 and its three consumers - role() at line 16, memberOf() at line 19 and the functions check at functions/index.js:48 - all verified.
This is the authorization model's root of trust, not a defence-in-depth measure.
No caller misuse is posited; the rule itself grants the write.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every read of the profiles document across the rules file and the functions, and matched each against the write rule that governs who may set the fields they read.

findings.title: The admin Cloud Function app has no authentication at all
findings.evidence: The `api` express app installs the bearer verifier - `api.use(requireIdToken)` (line 43). The `adminApi` app installs only CORS (line 72) and never installs requireIdToken or any equivalent. It is deployed as an onRequest function (line 111) and published at /admin/** by the hosting rewrite (firebase.json:7). Both of its routes use the Admin SDK, which bypasses Firestore rules entirely.
findings.impact: Anyone on the internet can call GET /admin/orgs/{orgId}/members to enumerate every member record of any organisation (line 75-76), and POST /admin/orgs/{orgId}/seats to rewrite that organisation's seatLimit (line 80). The CORS middleware reflects the caller's origin (line 15), so the member listing is also readable directly from any attacker-controlled web page.
findings.recommendation: Add `adminApi.use(requireIdToken)` and, beyond authentication, an explicit administrator authorisation check on both routes - the org id is a path parameter, so membership and role must both be verified.

triage.reason: Rule 02's carve-out covers local-only test functions; this is a deployed HTTPS function published through the hosting rewrite at firebase.json:7.
Verified that api.use(requireIdToken) appears at line 43 and that no equivalent appears for adminApi between lines 71 and 82.
Ingress cited: functions/index.js:75 `req.params.orgId` and line 80 `req.body.seatLimit`, both from an unauthenticated public HTTPS request.
functions/index.js is the deployed entrypoint declared in functions/package.json:5.

findings.title: exportOrgNotes callable checks neither authentication nor org membership
findings.class: Broken access control / bulk data exfiltration
findings.evidence: The callable takes orgId from the request data and validates only that it is non-empty (lines 89-92). It never reads `request.auth`, so unauthenticated invocation is not rejected, and it never checks that the caller belongs to the organisation - unlike the sibling REST route, which does exactly that check at lines 47-50. It then reads up to 5000 notes with the Admin SDK (line 94), which bypasses the Firestore rules.
findings.impact: Any caller who knows or guesses an org id can export that organisation's field notes in bulk - id, ownerId, status, title and body for up to 5000 records - regardless of authentication or membership. The doc comment acknowledges the export deliberately spans every inspector's notes, so this is the whole corpus for the org.
findings.recommendation: Reject when request.auth is absent, then check the caller's membership of orgId the same way the REST route does (reading the profile with the Admin SDK) before querying, and consider requiring an org-admin role for a bulk export.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: functions/index.js:89 `request.data?.orgId` on a public callable endpoint; the client invocation is at web/src/share.js:44.
Verified that request.auth appears nowhere in the callable body (lines 88-101), while the sibling route's membership check is present at lines 47-50.
This is a missing authorization check on bulk data access, not a hygiene omission.
The omission is in the callable itself.

scope.established_by: Diffed the callable against api.get('/notes/recent'), which reads the same collection: the REST route loads the caller's profile and tests org membership, the callable does neither.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by the LIMIT of 5000 applied at line 94, and by requiring knowledge of an org id - which the unauthenticated adminApi member listing also hands out.

findings.title: Recursive org wildcard grants every member full write over every other member's notes
findings.evidence: Nested inside /orgs/{orgId} is `match /{document=**} { allow read, write: if memberOf(orgId); }` (lines 45-47) - a recursive wildcard granting read and write on every document at any depth beneath the org to any member, with no role condition and no owner condition. Field notes live at exactly that path: web/src/notes.js:19 writes to `orgs/{orgId}/notes`, and both Cloud Functions read the same collection (functions/index.js:52, 94). The per-owner rules at lines 35-39 govern a different, top-level /notes collection and do not constrain this path.
findings.impact: Any member of an organisation can read, modify and delete every other inspector's field notes, contradicting the model stated at line 34 ('A field note belongs to the inspector who took it'). Because the note document carries the ownerId field, a member can also rewrite ownerId to their own uid - and the Storage rules then read that same field to decide who may download the note's attachments (storage.rules:9), so a rules-level note write converts into access to another inspector's evidence photos.
findings.recommendation: Replace the recursive wildcard with explicit per-collection matches, and gate writes under orgs/{orgId}/notes on `resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid` (with an admin exception if supervisors genuinely need it). Never allow a client to write the ownerId field that another rules file consults.

triage.reason: The wildcard at lines 45-47, the distinct top-level notes rules at lines 35-39, the client's write path at web/src/notes.js:19 and the Storage cross-reference at storage.rules:9 all verified.
Ingress cited: web/src/notes.js:45 updateDoc on `orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}` - a direct client SDK write authorised by this rule.
The over-broad grant is in the rule itself.
memberOf is a real check and is credited as bounding the attacker to the org - but the finding is precisely that membership alone is the whole condition.

scope.established_by: Determined which concrete collection paths the wildcard covers by listing every path the client and the functions actually write beneath /orgs/{orgId}/; notes is the one carrying per-owner semantics.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by memberOf(orgId) - the attacker must be a member of the target org, which the self-writable profiles document makes trivially satisfiable.

findings.title: Storage update rule lets any authenticated user overwrite any note attachment
findings.evidence: Within the attachment match block, read, create and delete are all conditioned on `noteOwner() == request.auth.uid` and create additionally caps size and content type (lines 12-17, 22). update carries only `if request.auth != null` (line 20) - no ownership check, no size cap, no content-type restriction.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user can overwrite any existing attachment on any note in any organisation, provided they can name the path. Because the size and MIME constraints that guard create are absent from update, the replacement can be of arbitrary size and arbitrary content type - including text/html, which the object's download URL will then serve, giving stored content execution on the storage origin. Overwriting inspection evidence photos is on its own an integrity failure for what is a compliance record.
findings.recommendation: Give update the same conditions as create: owner check, size cap and content-type match. If a rotate/crop re-upload is the use case, that operation is performed by the owner and satisfies the owner check.

triage.reason: Verified that lines 12, 14-17 and 22 all carry noteOwner() while line 20 carries only the null check.
Ingress cited: web/src/notes.js:61 uploadBytes to `orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}/{fileName}` - a direct client SDK write authorised by this rule.
The size and content-type caps are present on the sibling operation, so their absence here is an inconsistency in a control that exists, not a missing hardening measure.
The rule itself grants the write.

scope.established_by: Compared the four operation clauses in the same match block; three share one predicate and update alone drops it.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed to objects that already exist - update, unlike create, applies only to overwriting an existing path, so the attacker must know or guess the orgId/noteId/fileName triple.

findings.title: Audit trail documents can be overwritten through the seal endpoint
findings.evidence: The handler composes the audit document id entirely from request-supplied values - `const auditId = \`${orgId}_${seq}\`` (line 61), where both come from normalizeRequest(req.body) (line 60) - and writes with `db.doc(...).set(...)` (line 62), which replaces an existing document rather than failing. It runs under the Admin SDK, so the `allow write: if false` on /audits (firestore.rules:53) that makes the trail immutable for clients does not apply. The handler also never checks that the caller belongs to orgId or has any relationship to noteId.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user can overwrite an arbitrary existing audit record by supplying the org id and sequence number that compose its id, replacing its noteId and sealedBy fields with values of their choosing - destroying or falsifying the trail the rules file describes as immutable. They can equally write audit entries for organisations they do not belong to.
findings.recommendation: Use `.create()` so an existing id fails, derive the sequence number server-side (a transaction or a Firestore-generated id) rather than taking it from the body, and check the caller's membership of orgId and their relationship to noteId before writing.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: functions/index.js:60 normalizeRequest(req.body) supplies both orgId and seq, which compose the document id at line 61.
The id composition at line 61, the .set() at line 62 and the client-side immutability rule at firestore.rules:53 all verified.
normalizeRequest's character-class strip (line 34) sanitises the orgId for path safety but does not prevent it naming an existing document.
Immutability of the audit trail is a control this system explicitly implements at the rules layer; the finding is that the function layer bypasses it.

scope.established_by: Read the id derivation and the write verb, then checked which layer enforces audit immutability and whether the Admin SDK is subject to it.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed by requireIdToken on the api app (line 43): the caller must present a valid Firebase ID token, though it need not belong to the target org.

findings.title: Shared note body is assigned to innerHTML
findings.evidence: renderSharedNote uses textContent for the heading and for every metadata field (lines 9-11, 30) but assigns the note body directly: `article.innerHTML = note.body` (line 39). note.body is read from Firestore (line 20) and is written by the client with no sanitisation on either the create or the update path (web/src/notes.js:34, 45-48).
findings.impact: Any writer of a note body - which, per the recursive org wildcard, is every member of the organisation, and after profile self-elevation is effectively any signed-in user - stores script that executes in the browser of every recipient of the share link. The share link is described as being sent to an external site contact, so the payload runs for viewers outside the organisation, on the application's own origin, with the victim's Firebase session available to it.
findings.recommendation: Render the body as text, or sanitise it with a vetted library (DOMPurify) configured to the tag set the rich-text field actually produces, before assignment.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: web/src/notes.js:34 (createNote writes body verbatim) and web/src/notes.js:45-48 (updateNote spreads an unsanitised patch), reaching the sink at share.js:39 via the getDoc at line 20.
Verified that share.js uses textContent at lines 9-11 and 30 and innerHTML only at line 39.
No sanitiser is in use at all here - this is not a safe library applied without paranoia.
Both the unsanitised writer and the unsafe renderer are in this repository.

scope.established_by: Checked every DOM insertion in the file for its sink type; this is the only innerHTML assignment, and the surrounding code establishes that textContent was the author's default.

findings.title: CORS reflects any origin on both Cloud Function apps
findings.evidence: `cors({ origin: true })` (line 15) reflects whatever Origin the request carries back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. It is installed on both express apps (lines 42 and 72), so it applies to every response either app produces. The comment at lines 10-14 argues this is costless because callers authenticate with a bearer token rather than a cookie.
findings.impact: The reasoning holds for the `api` app: the browser will not attach a bearer token automatically, so reflection alone does not let a third-party page act as the victim. It does not hold for `adminApi`, which requires no credential at all - there, origin reflection means any web page can read the org member listing directly from the visitor's browser. Rated low because the underlying defect is the missing authentication rather than the CORS setting.
findings.recommendation: Replace `origin: true` with the explicit list of first-party and partner origins. This is secondary to adding authentication to adminApi.

triage.reason: Origin reflection is an affirmative permissive setting rather than an omitted hardening header - though the low severity reflects that on the bearer-authenticated app the author's reasoning is largely correct.
No adjacent class is invented; the impact claimed is confined to what origin reflection permits on the app that has no authentication.
The middleware construction at line 15 and both installations at lines 42 and 72 verified.
Ingress cited: the Origin header of any request to either app; the reflected value is returned at every response.

scope.established_by: The middleware is installed with app.use on both express instances, so it applies to every response from both - two installation sites rather than a per-route header. Listed both.
scope.narrowed_by: Narrowed on the `api` app by requireIdToken (line 43): the browser does not automatically attach an Authorization header, so reflection there does not by itself yield authenticated cross-origin reads. It is not narrowed on adminApi.
